-Analyst 1
```{r}
library(effectsize)
library(readr)
library(tidyverse)
my_data <- read_csv("C:/ELTE_ST/Additional_research_activity/gamedev/Schweinsberg/data/edge1.1.csv")
df <- dplyr::select(my_data, ThreadId:UniqueFemaleParticipation, Id_num, Female, Order)
# --------------------------------
d <- df %>% filter(Female_Contributions==UniqueFemaleContributors) %>% 
  group_by(ThreadId) %>%
  arrange(Order) %>%
  mutate(females_in_discussion=cumsum(Female), next_female =lead(Female)) %>%
  ungroup()
# --------------------------------
ggplot(data=d, aes(x=females_in_discussion, y=next_female))+
  geom_smooth()
# --------------------------------
#logistic regression model
model <- glm (next_female ~ females_in_discussion, data = d, family = binomial)
summary(model)
# --------------------------------
# Split d into 0-5 or 6- females in discussion based on the plot
d5 <- filter(d, females_in_discussion < 6)
d6 <- filter(d, females_in_discussion > 5)
# --------------------------------
model5 <- glm (next_female ~ females_in_discussion, data = d5, family = binomial)
summary(model5)
model6 <- glm (next_female ~ females_in_discussion, data = d6, family = binomial)
summary(model6)
# --------------------------------
# --------------------------------
library(MASS)
#odds ratio and confidence interval for the overall model
exp(confint.default(model))
exp(coef(model)) ##Reviewer 2 COMMENT: effect size as reported by analyst found here
# --------------------------------
#odds ratio and confidence interval for the "up to 5 females model"
exp(confint.default(model5))
exp(coef(model5))
# --------------------------------
#odds ratio and confidence interval for the "6 or more females model"
exp(confint.default(model6))
exp(coef(model6))
# --------------------------------
# --------------------------------



```


-Analyst 2
```{r}
#added libraries used:
library(dplyr)
library(effsize)
# --------------------------------
# Data from my_data, effectively a convience sample of "communication" or a cenus of the site, depending perspective
my_data <- read.csv("C:/ELTE_ST/Additional_research_activity/gamedev/Schweinsberg/data/edge1.1.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# --------------------------------
h1_data <- my_data %>%
  filter(Type == 2, #communications of type conversation
     	!is.na(Female), #gender is identified
     	Female == 1 #gender is Female
  ) %>%
  arrange(Year, ThreadId, Id_num, Order) %>%
  group_by(Year, ThreadId, Id_num) %>% #for each person in thread in year in order
  mutate(first_post = c(1, rep(0,n()-1)))  %>% # mark 1st post 1, others 0
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(Year, ThreadId, Order) %>%
  group_by(Year, ThreadId) %>% #for each thread in each year in order
  mutate(n_females = lag(cumsum(first_post)), #the cumlative sum at the entry above the
    	n_females = ifelse(is.na(n_females), 0, n_females) #current one is the number
 ) %>%   #of females at post time, so shifted down to current
 ungroup() %>%
  group_by(Year, ThreadId, n_females) %>% #for each sequence of the same number of females
  summarise(n_posts= n()) %>% #calculate the amount of activity
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(n_females > 0) #posts with no females can only have one post from a female before
# they become posts with one female, so discarding them as there is no variation.
# with a range of numeric values and numeric outcomes, I'm doinga linear regression
h1_result <- lm(n_posts ~ n_females, data=h1_data)
# --------------------------------
### reporting
# summary(h1_result)
```

```{r}
#load necessary packages
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
# --------------------------------
#read in data set
my_data <- read.csv("C:/ELTE_ST/Additional_research_activity/gamedev/Schweinsberg/data/edge1.1.csv")
# --------------------------------
# remove NA values
my_data <- my_data[complete.cases(my_data), ]
# --------------------------------
# the number of times a woman speaks in a specific conversation = "FemaleContributions"
# number of females in discussion = "Female" (1 = Female, 0 = Male)
# percentage of comments made by a woman = "FemaleParticipation" 
# --------------------------------
# Let's select columns only  related to the first hypothesis
female <- c("Female_Contributions", "Female", "FemaleParticipation")
my_data.1hyp <- my_data[, female]
# --------------------------------
#remove all NA rows
my_data.1 <- my_data.1hyp[complete.cases(my_data.1hyp), ]
# --------------------------------
# Let's remove all outliers from data 
# Through calculation from summary(my_data.1$FemaleParticipation)
# and summary(my_data.1$FemaleContributions), I got outlier values.
my_data.1 <- my_data.1 %>% 
  filter(FemaleParticipation < 0.20, Female_Contributions <= 22.5)
# --------------------------------
#plot FemaleContributions as a function of FemaleParticipation
(p <- ggplot(my_data.1, aes(y = Female_Contributions, x = FemaleParticipation)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F) +
  xlab("Female Participation") +
  ylab("Female Contribution"))
# --------------------------------
# --------------------------------
# summary
my_data.1_fit <- lm(Female_Contributions ~ FemaleParticipation, my_data.1) 
# --------------------------------
# get the correlation between Female Contributions and Female Participation
my_data.1 %>%
  summarize(r = cor(Female_Contributions, FemaleParticipation,
                    use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))
# --------------------------------
# Get residuals
my_data.1 <- my_data.1 %>%
  add_residuals(my_data.1_fit)
# --------------------------------
# Plot residuals in scatterplot
ggplot(my_data.1, aes(Female_Participation, resid)) +
  geom_ref_line(h = 0) +
  geom_point()
```


-Analyst 6
```{r}
#Test hypothesis 1: "A woman’s tendency to participate actively in the conversation correlates positively with the number of females in the discussion".
# --------------------------------
#Consider making this into a function?
library(tidyverse)
my_data <-read_csv("C:/ELTE_ST/Additional_research_activity/gamedev/Schweinsberg/data/edge1.1.csv")

my_data = read_csv("C:/ELTE_ST/Additional_research_activity/gamedev/Schweinsberg/data/edge1.2_anonymized.csv")

my_data = read_csv("C:/ELTE_ST/Additional_research_activity/gamedev/Schweinsberg/data/edge1.1_anonymized OLD dataset.csv")
# --------------------------------
counts <- my_data %>% group_by(Title) %>% summarise(count = n())
# --------------------------------
#Decisions: 
#1. Include all types of conversations (but consider analyzing them separately too.)
#2. Dependent variable: incidences of women speaking/total contributions
#3. Independent variable: percentage of contributors that are female.
# --------------------------------
#First, just test dependence of Fpart on UFPar - don't control for anything else.
fit_dat <- my_data %>% select(Title, UniqueFemaleParticipation, FemaleParticipation) 
fit <- lm(FemaleParticipation ~ UniqueFemaleParticipation, data = my_data)
summary(fit)
# --------------------------------
#So, a greater percentage of contributions come from women when a greater percentage of contributors are female; 
#for every 1% increase in % of contributors that are female, there is a 0.48% increase in fraction of comments coming from women. 
#This suggests that women contribute fewer comments per person than men, but doesn't really answer our question.
# --------------------------------
#One thing to try: for each individual woman in the dataset, calculate an average number of comments per discussion that she's in.
#Then, for those women, calculate how that summary statistic relates to number of women in a conversation.
women <- my_data %>% filter(Female == 1) %>% 
  select(Title, Name, Id, PreviousContributions, PreviousThreads, ContributionsThisYear, ThreadsThisYear) %>%
  group_by(Title, Id) %>% 
  summarise(comments_now = n(),
            PreviousContributions = mean(PreviousContributions),
            PreviousThreads = mean(PreviousThreads),
            cont_this_year = mean(ContributionsThisYear),
            threads_this_year = mean(ThreadsThisYear)) 
women <- women %>%
  mutate(total_previous_contributions = PreviousContributions + cont_this_year,
         total_previous_threads = PreviousThreads + threads_this_year)
# --------------------------------
#For each woman, get the number of contributions relative to her mean previous contributions.
women <- women %>% 
  mutate(cont_per_thread = total_previous_contributions/total_previous_threads) %>%
  mutate(comments_now_percent_change = (comments_now - cont_per_thread)*100/cont_per_thread)
# --------------------------------
#Now, for each conversation, get the number and percent of females. 
number_of_women <- my_data %>% 
  group_by(Title) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  dplyr::select(Title, UniqueFemaleContributors, UniqueFemaleParticipation)
# --------------------------------
#Join data for regression.
reg_dat <- left_join(women, number_of_women, by = "Title")
# --------------------------------
#Run regression. 
#First, a regression strictly against the hypothesis: that it depends on number of women. 
fit <- lm(comments_now_percent_change ~ UniqueFemaleContributors, data = reg_dat)
summary(fit)
#Results of regression suggest that the number of unique female contributors in a conversation negatively affects tendency to participate. 
#R2 is small (1.2%) and effect size suggests that for every extra woman active in a conversation, an individual woman is likely to comment 0.58% less than she has historically (p = 0.01)
#Make diagnostic plots:
plot(fit)
# --------------------------------
#Number 325 is an outlier in almost every way: look at that individual, and remove from regression.
View(reg_dat[325,])
#that individual participated very actively in one discussion after previously "lurking" 8 times. 
#Redo regression without her.
fit2 <- lm(comments_now_percent_change ~ UniqueFemaleContributors, data = reg_dat[-325,])
summary(fit2)
#Removing that outlier reduced the effect size (to -0.38), increased R2 to 1.9%, and decreased the p-value.
#diagnostic plots:
plot(fit2)
#Diagnostic plots are still imperfect, but better. Would also be good to try square-root/log transformations of predictors. 
# --------------------------------
#Log transformation:
fit3 <- lm(comments_now_percent_change ~ log(UniqueFemaleContributors),
           data = reg_dat[-325,])
summary(fit3)
plot(fit3)
#That improved R2; doesn't seem to have improved diagnostic plots enough to be worth the loss in interpetability 
#(e.g., effect size units are now much more difficult to interpret).
# --------------------------------
#Square root transformation:
fit4 <- lm(comments_now_percent_change ~ sqrt(UniqueFemaleContributors),
           data = reg_dat[-325,])
summary(fit4)
plot(fit4)
# --------------------------------
#Take a look at histogram of predictors just for reference:
ggplot(reg_dat, aes(x = UniqueFemaleContributors)) + geom_freqpoly(bins = 8)
# --------------------------------
#And plot percent change in comments against unique female contributors.
ggplot(reg_dat[-325,], aes(x = UniqueFemaleContributors, 
                           y = comments_now_percent_change)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5)
# --------------------------------
#This makes for a marginally significant but still negative trend. 
#These diagnostic plots look better, but I don't really believe in just removing those values. 
# --------------------------------
```

-Analyst 11
```{r}

library('readr')
library('lme4')
library('dplyr')
library(tidyverse)
# For each female participant, need to find out if 
# active in conversation or not.
# This is probably the crucial step that will change the 
# analysis results. As I have no prior experience about how
# to determine active participation, I will naively use the 
# number of contributions as a proxy.

# Load in data
my_data = read_csv('C:/ELTE_ST/Additional_research_activity/gamedev/Schweinsberg/data/edge1.1.csv')

# First, retrieve number of contributions to each conversation for
# female participants
particip.data = filter(my_data, Female==1) %>%
  group_by(ThreadId, Id) %>%
  summarize(ContributionsbyAuthor=unique(ContributionsbyAuthor),
            UniqueFemaleContributors=unique(UniqueFemaleContributors))

# Fit a random effects model with poisson link function to model
# the (count-data) outcome given the dependent variable
glmer.model = glmer(ContributionsbyAuthor ~ UniqueFemaleContributors + (1|ThreadId),
                    data=particip.data,
                    family=poisson)
# Print summary
summary(glmer.model) ##Reviewer 2 COMMENT: model used by analyst to report regression coefficient
standardize_parameters(glmer.model, exponentiate = TRUE)



```

```{r}
# create a thread-level data frame (1 row/thread)
threads <- my_data %>% 
  select(
    ThreadId,
    Type,
    DebateSize,
    Female_Contributions,
    Male_Contributions,
    UniqueContributors,
    UniqueFemaleContributors,
    UniqueMaleContributors,
    UniqueFemaleParticipation,
    Live
  ) %>% 
  distinct
# --------------------------------
# *restrictions?*
# -- limit the conversations to have at least 2 participants
# -- ensure that there is at least one female present in each thread
# this ensures we can at least measure a response
threads <- threads %>% 
  filter(
    UniqueContributors > 1,
    UniqueFemaleContributors >= 1
  )
# --------------------------------
# participation could be modeled as a binary outcome?
# with 1 indicating that the number of female contributions >= male contributions
threads$parity <- with(threads, as.numeric(Female_Contributions >= Male_Contributions))
# --------------------------------
## ^ this could work fine, but probably is highly sensitive to live/not-live?
## better to create two separate models?
# --------------------------------
# active participation (from women) would necessarily be marked by an increase in 
# the number of female contributions
# instead of a binary outcome, a count-based model could be used to model the
# number of contributions-- need to examine distribution of count
# --------------------------------
### plot distribution of female contribution by live/not-live
threads %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = FemaleContributions, fill = factor(Live))) +
  geom_density(alpha = .65)
# --------------------------------
View(threads)
# --------------------------------
# the thread-level data is not unique-- there are conversations that have 
# 2 observations per Thread ID. I'm assuming this reflects comments from people
# on transcriptions. I will code the status of these threads as live and
# deduplicate the frame; if there is any impact coming from the 'live' status,
# I believe it's more important to note the fact that the original event was
# a transcription rather than an essay/written work.
# --------------------------------
# if the thread is ever marked as live, set as 1, otherwise leave it as-is
# then, unique the data
threads <- threads %>% 
  group_by(ThreadId) %>% 
  mutate(
    Live_ever = as.numeric(ifelse(any(Live == 1), 1, Live)),
    live_and_not_live = as.numeric(n() > 1)
  ) %>% 
  select(-Live) %>% 
  ungroup %>% 
  distinct
# --------------------------------
# if Live_ever == 1, that means there's at least some aspect of the thread that
# was transcribed.
# live_and_not_live indicates the thread has a mix of transcribed and written 
# content
# --------------------------------
threads$prop_f_contributors <- with(threads, UniqueFemaleContributors / UniqueContributors)
threads$debsize_z <- with(threads, (DebateSize - mean(DebateSize)) / sd(DebateSize))
# --------------------------------
thread_fit_poisson <- glm(
  Female_Contributions ~
    Live_ever + 
    debsize_z +
    UniqueFemaleParticipation,
  data = threads,
  family = poisson
)
# --------------------------------
library(broom)
# --------------------------------
# get the incident rate ratios and their confidence intervals
irr <- thread_fit_poisson %>% 
  tidy %>% 
  bind_cols(confint_tidy(thread_fit_poisson)) %>% 
  select(term, estimate, contains("conf")) %>% 
  mutate_each(funs(exp), -term) %>% 
  mutate_each(funs(round(., 4)), -term)
# --------------------------------
# print
irr 
# --------------------------------
# plot the irr results, but make sure the points are on a log scale
irr %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = term, y = estimate, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_flip()
# --------------------------------
summary(thread_fit_poisson)
standardize_parameters(thread_fit_poisson, exponentiate = TRUE)
# --------------------------------
# deviance goodness of fit
pchisq(thread_fit_poisson$deviance, df = thread_fit_poisson$df.residual, lower.tail = FALSE)
# --------------------------------
# deviance table
anova(thread_fit_poisson, test = "Chisq")
# --------------------------------
res_thread_fit_poisson <- residuals(thread_fit_poisson, type = "deviance")
# --------------------------------
plot(log(predict(thread_fit_poisson)), res_thread_fit_poisson)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
# --------------------------------
qqnorm(res_thread_fit_poisson)
qqline(res_thread_fit_poisson)
# --------------------------------
mean(threads$FemaleContributions)
sd(threads$FemaleContributions)
# --------------------------------
# install.packages("margins")
# --------------------------------
```

```{r}
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
)


## read data
my_data <- read_csv("C:/ELTE_ST/Additional_research_activity/gamedev/Schweinsberg/data/edge1.1.csv")

## Test Hypothesis 1: A woman's tendency to participate actively 
## in the conversation correlates positively with the number of 
## females in the discussion.

## subset to just keep the conversation level data
d.conversation <- my_data %>% distinct(ThreadId, .keep_all = T) 

## create training, query, and test data sets to facilitate exploration
## to do this I need to select an outcome variable on which to split
## here, I use the percentage of female participation in that thread

set.seed(123)
trainIndex <- createDataPartition(d.conversation$FemaleParticipation, p = .6, 
                                  list = FALSE, 
                                  times = 1)

d.train <- d.conversation[ trainIndex,]
d.test  <- d.conversation[-trainIndex,]

## explore training data via visualization

# what's the distribution of female vs male contributions
d.train %>% 
  select(ThreadId, Male_Contributions, Female_Contributions) %>% 
  gather(gender, contributions, -ThreadId) %>% 
  ggplot(., aes(x = contributions, color = gender)) +
  geom_freqpoly(stat = 'density')

# what's the distribution of female participation
d.train %>% 
  distinct(ThreadId, .keep_all = T) %>% 
  ggplot(., aes(x = FemaleParticipation)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60) 

# what's the distribution of number of female and male contributors?
d.train %>% 
  distinct(ThreadId, .keep_all = T) %>% 
  select(ThreadId, UniqueMaleContributors, UniqueFemaleContributors) %>% 
  gather(gender, n_contributors, -ThreadId) %>% 
  ggplot(., aes(x = n_contributors, color = gender)) +
  geom_freqpoly() 
  
# now let's try to visualize the relationship between female participation and number of female contributors
d.train %>% 
  distinct(ThreadId, .keep_all = T) %>% 
  filter(UniqueFemaleContributors >= 1) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = UniqueFemaleContributors, y = FemaleParticipation)) +
  geom_boxplot(mapping = aes(group = cut_width(UniqueFemaleContributors, 1)),
               varwidth = F)

# visualize the same relationship but treating both as continuous variables 
d.train %>% 
  filter(UniqueFemaleContributors >= 1 & UniqueContributors > 1) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = UniqueFemaleContributors, y = FemaleParticipation)) +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess")

# fit linear model on training data
m1 <- d.train %>% 
  filter(UniqueFemaleContributors >= 1 & UniqueContributors > 1) %>%
  lm(FemaleParticipation ~ UniqueFemaleContributors, data = .)
standardize_parameters(m1)
summary(m1)

# fit linear model to test data

m1.test <- d.test %>% 
  filter(UniqueFemaleContributors >= 1 & UniqueContributors > 1) %>%
  lm(FemaleParticipation ~ UniqueFemaleContributors, data = .)
standardize_parameters(m1.test)
summary(m1.test) ##reviewer 2 COMMENT: Model used by analyst for reported results (hypothesis 1)

confint(m1.test, 'UniqueFemaleContributors', level=0.95)

## One more analysis where we subset the threads to only analyze
## "conversations" and remove "annual questions" that are asynchronous

d.train %>% 
  distinct(ThreadId, .keep_all = T) %>% 
  filter(UniqueFemaleContributors >= 1 & UniqueContributors > 1) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = UniqueFemaleContributors, y = FemaleParticipation, 
             size = UniqueContributors)) +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F) +
  facet_wrap(~Type, scales = "free_x")

# fit linear model including type of conversation to training data
m2 <- d.train %>% 
  filter(UniqueFemaleContributors >= 1 & UniqueContributors > 1) %>%
  lm(FemaleParticipation ~ UniqueFemaleContributors * Type, data = .)
 
summary(m2)

# fit linear model including type of conversation to test data
m2.test <- d.test %>% 
  filter(UniqueFemaleContributors >= 1 & UniqueContributors > 1) %>%
  lm(FemaleParticipation ~ UniqueFemaleContributors * Type, data = .)

standardize_parameters(m2.test)
summary(m2.test)
```
